studies.title: Settle What Is Between You
studies.meaning: A question about property is answered by lifting the property out of the argument. The bounties are declared to belong to God and the Messenger, which does not so much decide who receives what as dissolve the standing of the claims being pressed. Three instructions follow at once, and only the last concerns obedience. The first two are about the questioners themselves: be mindful of God, and repair what has gone wrong between you. The quarrel is treated as the graver problem.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a surah that runs through the encounter at Badr and its aftermath. The classical sources report that after the fighting the men disagreed over what had been gathered: those who pursued the retreating force, those who had stood guard, and those who fought in the line each argued a claim. The commentators name that dispute as the occasion of the ayah, and several early collections carry the report.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning something given over and above what is owed, the same root behind the word for a voluntary extra prayer. The name itself concedes that nothing here was anyone's due.
The verb for mending what has broken and making something sound again. It is used both of reconciling people and of reforming conduct, so a quarrel is described here in the vocabulary of repair work.
The Arabic idiom treats the space between people as a thing that can be in good or bad condition. What the ayah asks to be put right is not the men themselves but the relation running between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A raiding party in Arabia divided what it took by a customary reckoning everyone knew and nobody had written down, and arguments over shares were a standing cause of feud between allied clans. Men who fought side by side in the morning could be enemies by nightfall over a single camel. The community at Medina had been assembled from tribes recently at war with each other.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this surah is named after occurs in the Quran only in this one ayah, where it appears twice, and nowhere else at all. Its root is the same one that gives the word for a voluntary prayer offered beyond what is prescribed, which is why translators reach for words like bounty, addition or windfall rather than payment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage subordinates a question about ownership to a question about relationships. Assigning the property upward takes the dispute out of the register in which it was being conducted, since nobody can press a claim against God. And by setting the repair of what is between people directly beside mindfulness of God, the ayah treats the two as a single instruction rather than as a duty and a courtesy.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for repairing what is between people, and turns it into a standing rule.
Returns to the same property later in the surah and sets out how a portion of it is assigned.
Names reconciliation between people as one of the few things worth speaking privately to arrange.

studies.applyIt: There is a relationship of yours with a small unrepaired thing in it, probably about something owed or something assumed. Do not wait until you can prove you were right. Send the first message this week, and let it be about the relation rather than the item. The ayah puts the repair before the settlement, deliberately.

studies.title: Hearts That Tremble
studies.meaning: A definition is offered with a restrictive particle, so what follows is presented as what believers are rather than as one description among several. Three marks are given and all three are responses rather than actions: the heart moves when God is mentioned, faith increases when the ayat are recited, and reliance rests on the Lord. The commentators note that the first two are involuntary, which makes them a test of a person rather than an instruction to them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a surah that deals with the battle of Badr and the disagreement over its spoils that followed. The first ayah reports that dispute, and this description of believers arrives immediately afterwards, before anything is decided. The commentators read the placement as deliberate: a definition of faith is set down before the community's quarrel about property is addressed at all.

keyTerms.note: A verb for fear that moves the body, distinct from the general word for being afraid. It names the physical flinch rather than the attitude, which is why the heart is given as its subject.
The passive of the verb behind remembrance. The trigger is described as the bare mention of God, not a sermon or an argument, so the response is to a name rather than to a case being made.
From the root for appointing an agent to handle your affairs. It stands in the ongoing present, so reliance is described as a continuous relation rather than as a decision taken once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Badr had just been fought and won against odds nobody had expected to survive, and the community was now arguing over camels, weapons and captives. The men who had stood in that line were sitting in Medina dividing property. That is the setting into which a description of trembling hearts and reliance is placed, and everyone hearing it had been part of both scenes.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with a question about the spoils of war and answers it in a single line, then turns immediately to this description of believers before returning to the battle. Classical commentators note the structure: an argument about property is interrupted by a definition of faith, and the interruption is where the answer actually lies.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Faith is described by what happens to a person rather than by what they profess, which makes it something they can observe in themselves without being able to manufacture it. The second mark adds a further claim: the same text produces increase in some listeners and nothing in others, so the response is diagnostic of the hearer rather than of the words. Reliance then turns inward experience outward into how a person lives.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same trembling of hearts at God's mention, adding patience and prayer.
Says the same recitation increases some in faith while others ask which of them it added to.
Describes skins shivering at the recitation before softening to the remembrance of God.

studies.applyIt: Read or listen to a short passage you already know well, and afterwards ask one honest question: did anything move. Do not manufacture a feeling. The ayah treats that response as information about where you are, and the useful thing about information is that it can be true on a day when the answer is nothing at all.

studies.title: What Makes Belief Real
studies.meaning: A description running since the surah's second ayah finishes with two ordinary practices: standing in prayer, and giving out of what has been provided. Nothing dramatic is named and no quantity is set. The verdict that follows is unusually strong, calling these the believers in truth, and it lists three things they receive rather than one. Then the passage turns without warning to a march out from home, and concedes in the same breath that a group of the believers did not want to go.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the opening of a surah about the encounter at Badr and its aftermath. The expedition began as an attempt to intercept a returning caravan and became a confrontation with a much larger armed force sent out to protect it. The commentators report real reluctance among some of the believers once it became clear what they were facing, and the passage records that reluctance rather than smoothing it away.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something stand and holding it upright, used of a building or a leaning pole. Prayer is not described as performed but as maintained, which shifts the emphasis onto continuity.
Placed after the noun as an intensifier, it works like a stamp of certification on the description. It is not a comparison with other believers but a confirmation that the label actually applies.
An emphatic participle: not merely reluctant but marked as such by the grammar. Placing it inside the same sentence as the departure keeps the account honest about how that morning actually began.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marching out of Medina meant crossing roughly eighty miles of open country with limited water. The expedition had few mounts, and men took turns riding. Nobody had set out expecting a battle, since the plan concerned goods rather than fighting. Learning on the road that an armed force was coming to meet them changed the arithmetic entirely, and every man had a household waiting behind him.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence calling these the believers in truth occurs twice in the Quran and both times in this surah, here and again at 8:74. The first time the description behind it is prayer and spending; the second time it is emigration, struggle and the giving of shelter. Both occurrences are followed by forgiveness and a generous provision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets the definition of a believer at a level anyone can reach. Neither prayer nor giving is heroic and neither is quantified. What follows makes the point sharper: the same people who meet that description are immediately shown as reluctant. Belief is being defined by what is kept up rather than by what is felt, which is exactly why the reluctance disqualifies nobody.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same verdict at the close of the surah, with a different set of actions behind it.
Opens another passage with the same two practices, prayer and giving, as the marks of belief.
States the principle behind the concession here, that you may dislike what is good for you.

studies.applyIt: Look at your prayer this week not as five separate moments but as a structure you are keeping upright. Which one of them is the pole that keeps slipping? Name it, then decide the single practical change that would hold it: an alarm, a place, a person who prays it beside you. Nothing more ambitious than that.

studies.title: The One Without Thorns
studies.meaning: Two things are described and neither is denounced. Some argued after the matter had been settled, and the comparison offered for their state is precise: people being driven towards death with their eyes open. Then the choice they had hoped for is named. Two Meccan groups were possible, a loaded caravan and an armed column, and the wish had been for the one carrying no weapons. The passage says plainly that the divine intention ran the other way, towards settling a question rather than towards an easy gain.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the days before the encounter at Badr. A trading caravan returning from Syria was the original objective; when it slipped past, an armed force out of Mecca continued towards the wells at Badr regardless. The commentators report that some of the men argued for turning back, and that the argument carried on after the decision was made. The passage keeps the disagreement in the record rather than editing it out.

keyTerms.note: A verb form implying argument passing back and forth between two sides rather than a question asked once. Its root carries the sense of twisting a rope tight, so the picture is of a contested pull.

The verb used for driving livestock forward from behind. Applied to men going into battle it keeps their reluctance vivid, while the clause about looking on rules out any suggestion that they misunderstood.
The ordinary word for a thorn, extended in Arabic to weapons and to fighting strength. The caravan is identified as the group without thorns, which is why the wish had settled on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The caravan trade between Mecca and Syria moved goods worth years of ordinary income. A large returning caravan carried leather, raisins and silver, and taking one outright was a recognised kind of operation with recognised rules. That is what the men had come out for. What arrived instead was a body of armed men from their own city, including cousins and brothers, which is a different proposition altogether.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the ayah uses for the armed group is the everyday Arabic word for a thorn, and this is its only occurrence anywhere in the Quran. Arabic extends the word to weapons and to fighting strength, so the sentence separates the two Meccan groups the way a hand separates two branches: one can be taken hold of, one cannot.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets two intentions side by side and does not pretend they matched. The men wanted a safe gain; what was intended cost more and settled more. Neither is described dishonestly, and the human preference is not called shameful. What the passage establishes is that a desire can be entirely reasonable and still not be what is happening, and that the gap between them proves nothing has gone wrong.

crossReferences.why: States the general form of what happens here: disliking what is good for you, wanting what is not.
Describes the same day from another angle, saying the meeting could not have been arranged deliberately.
Reports a similar argument among believers on a later battlefield, and what was in their minds.

studies.applyIt: Think of a plan of yours that was replaced by something harder, and be honest about the version you had wanted. Do not rush to declare the harder one better. Hold both in view for a minute and notice that your preference was reasonable and simply was not what happened. That is the entire content of these two ayat.

studies.title: The Cry And The Answer
studies.meaning: The purpose named in the previous ayah is restated in the barest possible form, one verb for each side: to make the true stand and the false collapse. Then the passage moves back to the night before, and the register changes completely, from strategy to a cry for help. The verb chosen is the one used for calling out in extremity rather than the ordinary verb for asking. What comes back is a number, and the commentators differ over how it relates to the larger figures given elsewhere.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Before the fighting at Badr the classical sources report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) stood praying through the night and calling on God with unusual intensity, and that this reassurance came in answer. The community was outnumbered by roughly three to one and poorly equipped, with a small number of mounts between them. Several early collections carry the report of that night in closely similar words.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb for calling in extremity, from a root also connected with rain that arrives after drought. It is not the ordinary verb for asking, and it assumes the caller is already past managing alone.
From a root meaning to stretch or extend, the same one behind the word for a tide coming in. Help is pictured as a line being lengthened rather than as a rescue arriving out of nowhere.
From the verb for riding behind someone on the same mount. Commentators read it as rank behind rank or as one group following another, and record both readings without deciding between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Calling for help was a formal act in Arabia with its own vocabulary. A man under attack could shout the name of his clan, and the call placed an obligation on them; failing to answer was a disgrace remembered for years. Everyone present knew what it was to call out for people who might or might not come. On that night the whole reflex was pointed in one direction.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the angels here occurs only in this ayah in the whole Quran, and the commentators are divided over whether it means rank behind rank or group following group. The Quran also names other numbers in connection with this kind of help, three thousand and then five thousand at 3:124 and 3:125, and the classical discussion of how the passages fit together is long.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer given is not the removal of the danger. The men still fought, and the surah goes on to say that what they saw was made to look manageable rather than made safe. What the reply supplies is company. That distinction runs right through the Quran's treatment of prayer, where the response to a cry is more often presence than rescue, and the ayah that follows says so outright.

crossReferences.why: Says immediately what the reinforcement was actually for, and where help really comes from.
Gives the other numbers of angels, and the same explanation that it was reassurance.
States the general principle of which this night is one particular and very pressed instance.

studies.applyIt: Recall the last time you prayed with real urgency, not the tidy kind. Notice what actually changed afterwards. Often it is not the situation but your capacity to stand inside it. Tonight ask for one specific thing in plain language, then pay attention over the following week to what arrives rather than to what you requested.

studies.title: Made Only For The Heart
studies.meaning: The ayah narrows twice inside a single line. Arabic's strongest way of limiting a statement is to negate and then allow one exception, and this sentence does it in both halves. What the reinforcement was: nothing except good news and a settling of hearts. Where help comes from: nowhere except God. The two names that close the ayah then answer the question this raises. Strength explains why no instrument is needed; wisdom explains why one was nonetheless provided.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the account of Badr that occupies the first half of this surah. The community was outnumbered and had come out expecting to intercept goods rather than to fight. The commentators place this ayah as a comment on the promise of angelic help in the previous line, and read it as heading off a conclusion the men would otherwise have drawn from hearing that promise.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected with the skin, since news shows in the face before it reaches speech. The word names the effect a message has on a person rather than the content the message carries.
The verb for something reaching a settled stop, used of ground that levels out and of a bird folding its wings. It describes stillness arrived at after motion, not calm that was there all along.

A single word covers the helping and the winning, so Arabic does not separate the aid from its result. Made definite and placed under a restriction, it says that everything the word covers has one source.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Morale in a small force was everything, and commanders in Arabia knew it. Numbers were shouted, allies exaggerated, and war poetry recited to steady men in the hours before contact. The men at Badr had spent the night inside exactly that atmosphere. What this ayah does is take a piece of encouragement of precisely that kind and state openly what it was for, which is unusual in any account of a battle.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of names that closes this ayah, the Mighty and the Wise, occurs thirteen times in the Quran, and four of those occurrences are in this surah alone, at 8:10, 8:49, 8:63 and 8:67. Each of the four sits at the end of a passage where an outcome has just been taken out of human hands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah separates a cause from a comfort. The angels are described as doing something to the men rather than something to the enemy, which means the account of the day contains a psychological event as well as a military one. It also protects a reader from a common error: treating the visible means by which help arrived as the explanation of why it arrived at all.

crossReferences.why: Describes the other half of the same reinforcement, what the angels were told to do.
Names the sending down of tranquillity into hearts as its own kind of divine action.
Shows numbers failing on a later day, then the same settling sent down to steady people.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time help arrived through an obvious channel: a person, a phone call, a job. Notice how quickly you filed the channel as the reason. Spend a minute today separating the two, without denying the channel any credit. The habit this ayah is building is not suspicion of means but accuracy about where they sit.

studies.title: Sleep, Water And Firm Ground
studies.meaning: Four things arrive in one sentence and only the first two are physical. Drowsiness comes over the men and is called a security, which inverts what sleep means on the eve of a fight. Then water falls, with four purposes listed for it: to wash them, to take away a defilement attributed to Satan, to bind something over their hearts, and to make their feet firm. Commentators read the last as literal ground and as steadiness of nerve at once, and decline to choose between them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the night before the fighting at Badr. The classical accounts describe the smaller force camped on loose sand near the wells while the larger one held better ground, and report rain falling that night. The passage lists what the weather did and narrates none of the battle. The commentators treat the physical details as reported facts and read the inward effects alongside them rather than in place of them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for draping something across a surface, used of a cloth laid over an object. Sleep is described as arriving from outside and settling on the men rather than as rising up within them.
A noun from the root for safety and trust. Naming drowsiness a security inverts the ordinary reading, since losing alertness before a fight is normally the danger rather than the relief.

keyTerms.gloss: and so that He may bind
keyTerms.note: The verb for tying something fast, used of tethering an animal. Binding upon the heart is an idiom for holding a person together under strain, and the same root names the tethering of horses at 8:60.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water decided everything in that country. The wells at Badr were the reason both forces were there at all, and whoever held them held the encounter. Sand that has been rained on packs down and carries weight, while dry sand swallows a foot at every step. Men who had walked to the site knew that difference in their legs before anybody explained it to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical accounts of the day report that the same rain did opposite things to the two forces, firming the loose sand where the smaller one stood and turning the ground under the larger one heavy. The ayah narrates none of that. It lists four purposes for the water, three of them inward, and leaves the tactics to the historians.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah pairs an inward gift with an outward one and refuses to rank them. Sleep and rain both arrive from outside the person, both are named as acts of God, and both are given plainly practical descriptions. That declines the division between spiritual help and material help. It also treats the body's condition as part of the account, since firm feet and a steadied heart appear in one series with one source.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same experience of sleep coming over a force, in nearly identical wording, on a later day.
Gives the ordinary use of rain sent down for cleansing and for reviving dead land.
Uses the same root for tethering later in the surah, applied there to horses rather than hearts.

studies.applyIt: Notice, for one day, how much of your steadiness is physical: sleep, water, food, solid ground underfoot. When something frightening is coming, the first honest question is often whether you have slept. This ayah puts drowsiness and rain in the same list as a heart being held together, without any apology for it.

studies.title: I Am With You
studies.meaning: The instruction is given to angels rather than to men, which is the first thing to register. It opens not with an order but with a statement of company. What the angels are told to do for the believers is to make them firm, an inward act, and what is said about the other side is also inward: dread placed in hearts. Only then come the two clauses about striking, which the classical commentators read as continuing the address to the angels in that particular engagement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, describing the encounter at Badr. The classical sources connect the ayah to the reports of angelic presence at that battle, and it sits in a passage recounting the day from several angles at once. The commentators are careful about the addressee, reading the verbs as still directed at the angels rather than turning to the human force. The surah's instructions to people are given separately a few ayat later.

keyTerms.note: The verb for fixing something so it cannot shift, used of a peg driven into ground. The angels' first assignment is described as steadying people rather than as fighting on their behalf.

A word for fear that seizes all at once and fills a person, distinct from ordinary apprehension. The Quran attributes it directly to God several times, always as something placed in hearts rather than produced by events.
The plural of the word for a neck. Arabic uses it in idioms for submission and for leadership, but the phrase here is a plainly physical battlefield description belonging to one specific day.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fighting in that world was close, brief and personal. Lines met within a few paces and men recognised the faces opposite them, since both sides came from the same handful of towns. A battle was usually decided less by casualties than by the moment one side's nerve broke and it turned. That is why an account of the day spends more words on hearts than on weapons.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran attributes this particular word for dread to God rather than to circumstances every time it uses it, in this ayah and in a small number of others describing later engagements. The grammar is consistent across all of them: the fear is cast or thrown into hearts, using verbs of placing, never verbs of causing or of frightening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes a battle largely as an event happening inside people. Believers are steadied and opponents filled with dread, and both are attributed to God rather than to anything either force did. That does not make the fighting unreal; it puts the decisive factor somewhere the participants could not inspect. It also places the angels under instruction, which keeps them creatures carrying out an order rather than powers of their own.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for dread cast into hearts, in the account of a different engagement.
Explains what the angelic presence was for, immediately before this description of what it did.
Names the opposite gift, tranquillity sent down on people, in a later account of a hard day.

studies.applyIt: The first thing the angels are told to do is steady people. Do that for someone this week. Not advice and not a solution: presence, and a sentence that says you are not going anywhere. Most people facing something hard need their nerve held more than their problem solved, and the difference usually shows within a minute.

studies.title: Standing On The Other Side
studies.meaning: A reason is supplied for what has just been described, and the word chosen for opposition is spatial: to take up the far side of a line. The general rule is then stated, so the particular case becomes one instance of it. The third ayah changes addressee entirely and speaks to the believers about a battlefield, and what it asks for is holding the line while two forces advance towards each other. The passage is describing what held that community together under pressure.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, within the account of Badr. The instruction in the third ayah belongs to a specific kind of engagement, where lines closed on open ground and one man turning could unravel an entire formation. The commentators discuss at length whether the instruction was tied to that day or wider, and they record the discussion rather than settling it. The ayah immediately after names two exceptions to it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a side or a half. Opposition is described as placing yourself on the other side of a line, which makes the word about position rather than about the temperature of a feeling.

The verb for tasting, used across the Quran of punishment. It converts something abstract into something that reaches a person directly, and it implies first-hand knowledge rather than being told about it.
A word for creeping or crawling forward, used of a large body of men moving as one. It names the interval before contact, when both sides are visible and closing and nobody has struck yet.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribal fighting line held only as long as each man believed the men beside him would stay. There were no ranks, no officers, and no penalty a commander could impose afterwards. What kept a line together was the certainty that anyone who ran would be named in poetry for the rest of his life, and that his family would carry the name after him.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the mass advance in the third ayah occurs only here in the Quran, and it is a word for slow creeping movement rather than a charge. Arabic uses it of a large body shifting forward together, which is what a seventh-century line actually did. Nothing in the passage describes speed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage gives a reason before it gives an instruction, which is this surah's habit throughout. Naming opposition in spatial terms, as taking the far side of a line, keeps the account from resting on motives nobody can inspect. Placing the address to the believers immediately after makes a further point: both sides of the conflict are being measured by the same standard rather than by two different ones.

crossReferences.why: Names the two exceptions to the instruction given here, in the very next ayah.
Gives the positive form of the same instruction: stand firm, and remember God much.
Uses the identical clause about opposing God and the Messenger, in a quite different setting.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you left a difficult situation early: a conversation, a commitment, a room. Not to judge it, but to notice which it was. Repositioning, regrouping, or simply going. The passage takes the first two seriously enough to name them a line later. Being honest about which one you did is the work here.

studies.title: Except To Turn And Fight
studies.meaning: A hard sentence with two doors cut into it. Whoever turns his back on that day is described as coming home carrying anger from God, and then two exceptions are named which change how the whole thing reads. Turning aside for the fight, and moving to join another group, are both movements away that are not flight. Commentators disagree over whether the statement applies to that day alone or beyond it, and they hold the disagreement in the open rather than resolving it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly from the previous ayah and belonging to the account of Badr. The phrase naming that day is what the disagreement turns on. Some commentators read it as limiting the statement to the battle in question; others as a way of saying any day of that kind. Both readings are old, and the classical commentaries record them side by side without treating either as settled.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning an edge or a side. It describes moving off the straight line for a purpose, which is why this movement is separated from flight by intention rather than by direction.
From the root for occupying a space. It names moving towards where other people are, so a man who leaves alone and a man who leaves to reach his own side are not doing the same thing.

The verb for returning home with something in hand. It makes the anger a thing brought back rather than a sentence pronounced, which is how the Quran generally describes what people bring upon themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian fighting was fluid. Small groups broke off, circled, regrouped and re-entered, and the distance between a manoeuvre and a rout could be a few seconds and a man's intention. Everyone watching believed they could tell the difference, and everyone could be wrong. The exceptions in this ayah are written by someone who knew what a battlefield actually looks like from inside it.
studies.didYouKnow: Both words naming the exceptions occur only in this ayah and nowhere else in the Quran. They are technical, drawn from the vocabulary of movement in a fight: one from the root for an edge or flank, the other from the root for taking up a space. Neither has any moral colour of its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The severity and the exceptions belong together. A statement without them would have made every tactical movement a moral failure; a statement without the severity would have handed every frightened man a cover story. What the ayah establishes is that one physical act can be two entirely different things, and that the difference lies in a purpose which only the person and God can actually see.

crossReferences.why: States the instruction that this ayah immediately qualifies with two named exceptions.
Describes people who did turn away on a later day, and what is said about them afterwards.
Addresses the calculation behind flight rather than its conditions, during a later siege.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between stepping back to think and walking out, and you know which one you have been doing with a particular problem. Name it accurately to yourself today, in a single sentence, without deciding anything else yet. The two exceptions exist in this ayah because the difference is real and invisible from outside.

studies.title: You Did Not Throw
studies.meaning: A victory is described by taking it away from the people who won it, and then the sentence does something stranger still. It denies an act and affirms it in one breath: you did not throw when you threw. The classical commentators read this as separating the motion from its effect, granting the man the movement and withholding the outcome. The stated purpose then arrives as a testing of the believers by something good, which makes the victory itself the trial rather than its reward.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources connect the second clause to a reported moment at Badr when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) took a handful of dust or gravel from the ground and threw it towards the opposing line. Several early collections carry the report, and the commentators treat it as the occasion of the phrase. The wider denial about the killing is read as covering the whole engagement.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for throwing or shooting. Its appearance three times in one short clause, first denied, then affirmed, then reassigned, is what makes the sentence famous among commentators on Arabic style.
The noun ordinarily means an affliction, and pairing it with the adjective for what is beautiful is deliberate. It says that being handed a victory is itself a form of being tested.
An active participle from the root for feebleness. What is described as weakened is not the men opposite but their planning, so the claim concerns a scheme losing its force rather than casualties.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Badr was fought on sand between low rises, and dust was the one thing that ground offered without limit. At close quarters, wind-carried grit in the eyes was a genuine nuisance and everyone had experienced it. A handful of it thrown towards a line could not injure anybody, and nobody present would have thought otherwise. That ordinary fact is what makes the sentence about the throw so pointed.
studies.didYouKnow: The short clause in the middle of this ayah uses one verb three times in a row: denied, then affirmed, then reassigned to God. Arabic grammarians and commentators have written a great deal about how a single act can be negated and confirmed inside one sentence, and the usual explanation separates the motion, which was a man's, from the effect, which was not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say that human action is unreal. The throw happened, the fighting happened, and the men are addressed throughout as the ones who did it. What is denied is the causal weight people naturally assign to their own effort. That leaves human action fully required and fully insufficient at the same time, which is the position the Quran keeps returning to whenever effort and outcome are discussed together.

crossReferences.why: States the same relation between a human act and its maker, well away from any battlefield.
Makes the parallel statement about victory, that it comes from God and nowhere else.
Describes another part of the same day, where even what people saw was arranged.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you did well recently and describe it twice: once as your own effort, honestly and without false modesty, and once as a set of conditions you did not arrange, such as health, timing, or the person who mentioned your name. Both accounts are true. This ayah holds them in one sentence, and so can you.

studies.title: The Verdict You Asked For
studies.meaning: The address turns to the other side and answers a request they had made. They asked for a decision; the passage tells them one has been delivered. Then two conditional sentences run in parallel: stop and it is better for you, come back and so will We. Offer and warning are given in the same grammatical shape, which sets them on equal footing. The closing clause explains why numbers will not help, and it is not a claim about relative strength.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources report that before the fighting at Badr one of the Meccan leaders prayed publicly at the Sacred House for God to decide between the two parties and destroy whichever was more in the wrong. The commentators connect this ayah to that request. The verb used for asking is built on the root for opening, which Arabic also uses for asking a judge to open a case.

keyTerms.note: From the root for opening. Arabic uses this form for asking a judge to open a case and hand down a ruling, so the request was for the matter to be settled rather than for help in winning.
The same root as the verb just before it, which is why the reply lands as it does. The word later becomes the ordinary Arabic term for a conquest, and names a whole surah.
A word for a group that stands together, used throughout this surah of both sides. Saying it will not avail however numerous makes the point about relation rather than about size.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths and appeals made at the Sacred House carried weight across the Hijaz, whatever a listener believed. A man who called publicly on God to judge between two parties was staking his standing on the answer, and the audience remembered such words and repeated them afterwards. Asking for a verdict in that setting was not a private prayer. It was a public wager with witnesses.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind both the request and the reply here, meaning to open, later names surah 48, where the same word describes a settlement reached without a battle. The Quran uses this root for opening a door, opening a case for judgement, and opening a city, and lets the three senses run into one another rather than keeping them apart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a request seriously and answers it, which is the striking part. A prayer made against the believers is treated as a genuine prayer and given a genuine reply. It also holds the door open in the same breath as it warns, and the offer comes first in the sentence. That ordering, desist before return, is how this surah handles its opponents throughout.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same offer to the same audience: desist, and what is past will be forgiven.
Records another prayer made by the same side, asking for stones to fall from the sky.
Uses the same verb for seeking a decision, applied there to an earlier community.

studies.applyIt: Be careful about the arguments you ask to have settled. Most of us pray to be proved right without quite meaning it literally. Pick one dispute you have wanted a verdict on, and ask honestly whether you would accept the answer if it went the other way. If not, you were asking for something else.

studies.title: Hearing Without Hearing
studies.meaning: Three ayat turning on a single verb. The first asks for obedience and adds a clause that makes turning away worse: while you are hearing. The second names people who said the right sentence and did not do what it describes, so the saying is itself the failure. The third delivers a verdict in the harshest terms this surah uses, and the fault it names at the end is not deafness but the refusal to reason. Commentators note that the deafness described is chosen rather than physical.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's account of the year of Badr. The community was newly assembled and its instructions travelled by voice, delivered and repeated aloud. The commentators report no single occasion and read the passage as addressing both those slow to act on what they had been told and, in the second ayah, opponents who claimed to have listened. The ayat sit between a battle account and an appeal to the community.

keyTerms.note: A present tense describing something still going on. Turning away is faulted not in general but specifically while the words are still arriving, which makes the timing part of what is wrong with it.
The plural of a word for anything that walks the earth, from a verb meaning to creep along. It is deliberately wide, covering animals and people together, and this surah uses the phrase twice.

The verb comes from the word for a tether used to hobble a camel. Reasoning is binding things so they do not wander off, which makes its absence a kind of looseness rather than a shortage of information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Medina moved by ear. Announcements were called out, agreements were witnessed by listeners, and poetry was the medium of both argument and record. A man's competence was measured partly by how well he held what he had heard once. In that setting, claiming to have heard and then acting as though you had not was a recognised and shameful kind of failure.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the worst of creatures occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, at 8:22 and again thirty-three ayat later at 8:55. The wording is identical up to the point where the description begins. The first names people who do not reason; the second names people who break every agreement they make.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the failure in reception rather than in access. Everybody in the scene heard the same words. What separates them is what happened after the sound arrived, and the closing verb makes that a matter of using the mind rather than of holding the right information. It also makes a claim about language: saying that you have understood is named as the very thing that can conceal not understanding.

crossReferences.why: Records the same split between the words said and the action taken, in an earlier community.
Extends the picture of working faculties left unused, and arrives at the same verdict.
Shows the kind of hearing that leaves nothing behind, in a later Medinan setting.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have heard repeatedly and agreed with and have never acted on. A single specific thing. Do the smallest version of it today, before you hear it said again. The passage is not against listening. It is against the particular comfort of feeling that agreeing is already a kind of doing.

studies.title: The Call That Gives Life
studies.meaning: The summons is described by its effect: responding is called being brought to life, which assumes the hearer is not fully alive without it. Then a sentence that stops the passage. God comes between a person and their own heart, which the commentators read as His power over the inner life and as a warning that a heart is not securely one's own possession. The second ayah widens the frame, since the trial named does not fall only on those who caused it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the surah dealing with Badr and its aftermath. The community was newly consolidated and its internal disagreements were beginning to have consequences beyond the people involved. The commentators read the warning about a trial reaching more than the wrongdoers as addressed to that situation, and preserve reports of early Muslims applying it to conflicts that arose later.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to answer that implies compliance rather than mere reply. The same word is used of God answering a supplication, so the human answer is put in the vocabulary usually reserved for His.
A verb for interposing and for change, used of standing between two things to keep them apart. Its ambiguity is preserved by the commentators, who read both separation and transformation in it.
Originally the assaying of gold by fire to separate it from what is mixed in. The word covers testing and the civil strife that tests a community, and both senses are active in this warning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal conflict spread by design. A dispute between two men obliged their clans, and allies were drawn in by prior oaths, so a quarrel that began at a well could end with settlements burned. Nobody in that world imagined a fight staying private. The warning about a trial that does not confine itself to the guilty described a mechanism the audience had watched work all their lives.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about God coming between a person and their heart is one of the shortest in the Quran to have generated a long commentary tradition, with readings ranging from His knowledge of what is hidden to His power to turn a heart in a new direction. Classical authorities record the range without settling it, and the ambiguity is generally treated as intended.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies a comfortable assumption, that whatever else is uncertain a person at least owns their own inner life. Placing God between someone and their heart removes that last private ground, and it does so in the middle of a call to respond, so the urgency is practical: what can be done now may not stay available. The second ayah then removes another comfort, that consequences stay with the people who earned them.

crossReferences.why: Describes being brought to life from death and given a light to walk by.
Asks that hearts not be turned aside after guidance, which assumes that they can be.
Applies the warning about discord directly to a community losing its strength.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good intention you have been carrying for months without acting on. Do the first physical step today, however small, before the intention gets any older. The warning here is not about wickedness. It is about the distance that can open between a person and what they meant, and how quietly that happens.

studies.title: A Criterion To Tell By
studies.meaning: A condition and three results. If you keep awareness of God, you are given a criterion, your bad deeds are covered over, and you are forgiven. The commentators explain the first as a capacity to distinguish, a discernment that comes with practice rather than with study. The order is worth noticing: the gift of telling things apart is named before the erasure of what is past, so clarity arrives as a consequence rather than as a reward for being clear already.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the surah on Badr, in a passage that recalls the community's earlier weakness in Mecca and the shelter given to it afterwards. The ayah sits between reminders of past vulnerability and warnings about betraying trusts. The commentators record no specific occasion, and read it as a general promise placed where the community most needed a way of judging difficult situations for itself.

keyTerms.gloss: a criterion, a means of separating
keyTerms.note: From the root for splitting apart. The same word names the day of Badr elsewhere in this surah and is used of revelation, so it covers anything that divides truth from its counterfeit.

From a root meaning to cover, the same one behind the word for a farmer who buries seed. Wrongs are described as covered rather than undone, which commentators keep distinct from the forgiveness named next.
What exceeds what is owed. Naming it at the end frames all three results as gifts rather than as payments, even though the sentence opened with a condition attached to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Judging situations without institutions was a daily skill. A merchant assessed a partner's honesty on a handshake, a traveller decided whom to trust on a road, a tribe weighed whether a peace offer was genuine. There were no records to consult and no authority to appeal to. Discernment was the practical faculty that kept people alive, and a promise of better discernment landed as a promise of safety.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for criterion appears in this surah twice with different references: once here as something given to a person, and once as a name for the day of Badr itself, the day of separation. It also titles surah 25 and is used of revelation elsewhere, so one term names a book, a day and a faculty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moral clarity is presented as the fruit of conduct rather than its precondition. That reverses the usual assumption, in which a person must first know what is right and then act on it; here, acting with awareness produces the capacity to tell. The claim is not that God supplies information, but that the faculty of distinguishing sharpens with use. Forgiveness follows, which keeps the promise from depending on having judged correctly so far.

crossReferences.why: Attaches a similar promise to the same condition, a way out and provision from nowhere.
Ends with the same construction, teaching following from awareness of God.
Uses the same word as the name of the day the two forces met at Badr.

studies.applyIt: Take one decision this week where you are genuinely unsure, and before you weigh the options, do something small you know is right and have been putting off. Then come back to the decision. The ayah puts the order that way round, and the claim is testable in a single afternoon.

studies.title: Your Wind Will Go
studies.meaning: Three instructions with a consequence set between them. Obey, do not quarrel with one another, and be steadfast, and the middle one carries the weight: internal dispute is said to produce two effects, losing heart and losing your wind. The commentators explain the second as the force that carries a group forward, and the image is meteorological rather than martial. The closing clause names what steadfastness gets, and it is company rather than victory.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from the section of the surah giving instruction for confrontation, after the account of Badr. Disagreements over strategy and over the division of gains had already appeared, and the surah opens with one of them. The commentators read this ayah as addressing that pattern directly rather than as general advice, and the warning against disputing comes before the call to endure.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form of the verb to snatch or pull. The image is of two parties tugging the same thing in opposite directions, which is why the result described is a loss of forward movement.
A verb for weakness arising from within rather than from an opponent. It names failure of nerve specifically, and it is placed as the immediate result of the quarrel rather than of anything external.
The ordinary word for wind, used of a group's force and standing. Commentators explain it as the impetus that carries people along, and a becalmed vessel is the picture behind it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab forces were coalitions of clans, each with its own leader, its own honour to protect and its own view of when to fight. Armies dissolved when one contingent withdrew, and a public argument between leaders could empty a field before anything began. Everyone hearing this had watched a gathering come apart that way. The warning described the ordinary cause of defeat, not an exotic one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the momentum a community loses is the everyday word for wind, and the Quran uses the same word elsewhere for the winds that carry rain and for the gale that destroyed an earlier people. Choosing it here makes a group's cohesion something like weather: real, forceful, and impossible to hold once it has turned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Internal disagreement is treated as a material cause with material effects, not as a moral failing to be regretted afterwards. The sequence is precise: quarrelling produces loss of nerve, and loss of nerve produces loss of force. Steadfastness is then named as the remedy, and what it earns is stated as company rather than as an outcome, which is a smaller promise than victory and a considerably more reliable one.

crossReferences.why: Commands holding to the same rope together and recalls the hearts that were joined.
Traces a reverse at Uhud to failure of nerve and dispute over an order.
Uses the same closing formula, that God is with those who are patient.

studies.applyIt: In the next group you are part of that is stuck, resist the urge to win the argument for one more meeting and instead ask what everyone actually agrees on. Say that list out loud. The ayah treats disagreement as something that drains a shared force, and naming the common ground is the cheapest way to stop the draining.
